::: {.welcome}
Solar and farming want the same flat, open, well-drained ground. An array can carry pollinator habitat or gravel, slow runoff or redirect it, shade stock, retire irrigation demand, or help sustain a farm. Those are design decisions.

**Agrisolar** names solar generation on agricultural land, whether or not production continues below it. **Agrivoltaics** is the narrower case of crops or livestock inside the footprint. Direct crop production under or between panels remains a small share of built practice [@stid2022; @macknick2022].

**Restorative agrisolar design** holds that ecological, hydrological, and community function belong among a project's objectives. This document gives that claim a vocabulary that can be tested on real ground.
:::

## A shared language

A solar grazier, township planner, hydrologist, and developer can describe the same eighty acres in incompatible terms. This lexicon is for the people deciding what an array does to an operation and a place.

A net-zero grid by 2050 could put solar on 60,000–90,000 km², roughly 1% of the contiguous United States [@larson2021]. Much of it will be farmland.

## How the language works

Three questions organize the document.

![How the pieces fit. Scale, sharing–sparing, and the design pressures resolve into an archetype and the functions it carries, with regionality setting how hard each pressure pushes.](figures/fig_language_structure.svg)

### Scale

Scale comes first because it settles what is physically, economically, and institutionally
possible before design begins. The [scale transect](chapters/1-the-scale-transect.qmd) runs
from the farmstead to the region in five zones. It is a transect rather than a set of size bins
because several things move together along it.

::: {.zone-table}
| Zone | Indicative footprint | What changes at this size |
|---|---|---|
| **A1 — Farmstead** | under ~1 acre | One owner-operator, existing farm labor, behind the meter |
| **A2 — Field** | ~0.5–8 acres | Still the landowner's decision, perhaps one lease counterparty |
| **A3 — Parcel** | ~5–80 acres | Multi-party; ground-layer management becomes a contract |
| **A4 — Landscape** | ~60–400 acres | Developer-led; grazing and habitat become enterprises |
| **A5 — Regional** | ~300 to 10,000+ acres | Transmission, institutional capital, many jurisdictions |
:::

Building-mounted arrays sit at the origin because they take no ground. Where capacity and acreage disagree, land area is the better guide to the design problem.

### Land sharing and land sparing

The accounting does not stop at the fence. **Land sharing** keeps production going on the same ground the array occupies. **Land
sparing** takes ground out of production so that other ground can be left alone. The pair comes
from a long-running argument in conservation ecology [@green2005; @phalan2011], where the
underlying question is genuinely unsettled: farm gently everywhere, or intensively in some places
and not at all in others.

The [sharing–sparing axis](chapters/2-the-sharingsparing-axis.qmd) runs five positions on that logic.

::: {.position-table}
| Position | What it records |
|---|---|
| **S1 — Full sharing** | Production continues in the same ground, inside the footprint |
| **S2 — Functional sharing** | The ground layer is productive but subordinate: grazing, forage |
| **S3 — Coexistence** | *Neither.* Production stops on that ground, and the revenue sustains the farm enterprise that holds it |
| **S4 — Idled-land sparing** | The array takes ground already idle or marginal, sparing land that is not |
| **S5 — Impaired-land retirement** | Production ends on ground that was carrying a burden off-site |
:::

The center is where most projects sit: ordinary ground becomes a power plant. A position records what happened to the ground, not the project's merit.

### Design pressures

Scale and position describe a site; nine [design pressures](chapters/3-design-pressures.qmd) explain why it takes that form. They conflict, have direction, and have advocates. The document argues that restorative goals belongs among them.

![Nine pressures bearing on one site at once, grouped by the direction they push. Three push toward restoration, three push away, and three depend on the site, the buyer, or the county.](figures/fig_design_pressures.svg)

The resulting [restorative functions](chapters/4-restorative-functions.qmd) are a palette, not a scorecard. Recurring resolutions become [archetypes](chapters/5-archetypes.qmd), from solar prairie strips to barnyard shelter, and can be compared in the same language.

::: {#sec-aim-not-dimensions}
The same pressures meet very different ground. Sun, water, crop, and grid conditions change their weight. **The aim is argued; the dimensions are left to the site**, and [regionality](chapters/6-regionality.qmd) explains why.
:::

## Where to start

::: {.routes}
**If you have land in mind and want to know what is possible on it**, go to
[what appears at each scale](chapters/5-archetypes.qmd#sec-by-zone), which sets out the forms that
recur at each size of project, from a barn roof to a regional complex, with what each one asks of the
ground.

**If you are weighing a specific proposal**, the
[design pressures](chapters/3-design-pressures.qmd) name the forces pushing on it and the
conflicts worth arguing about openly.

**If you are trying to pin down a term** someone has used, the
[alphabetical index](chapters/index-alphabetical.qmd) lists everything this document defines,
and the search box at the top of every page finds the rest.

:::

## Joining in

This is a working document, and it improves by being disagreed with. Corrections,
counterexamples, and proposed terms are welcome as issues or pull requests on
[GitHub](https://github.com/MSUHydrogeology/agrisolar_lexicon). Especially useful: an archetype
that recurs in your region and is missing here, a term that lands badly with the people who have
to use it, or a citation you can trace further than we have.
